newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich says will pull Republican 'team' together.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich says will pull Republican 'team' together.

text.p: With questions of loyalty to his leadership still open, House Speaker Newt Gingrich said Monday he will use his authority "in whatever way is needed" to bring Republicans together again as a team.

Commenting on the party's internal disputes and an attempt to overthrow him by some disgruntled conservatives, Gingrich said chaos and turmoil were to be expected given the amount of changes in government Republicans have tried to accomplish.

"As speaker of the House, I am in essence the head coach of House Republicans," he said. "It's the head coach's job to lead the team and to remind them, firmly if necessary, that we are after all a team and that we must pull together, in spite of differences or disputes that may exist."
"That is a message I will deliver -- in whatever way is needed -- to insure that our team works together as a team," he told a group of Marietta, Georgia business leaders.
Excerpts of his remarks given in Georgia Monday were made available by his Washington office.

House Republican leaders were to meet formally Tuesday afternoon for the first time since the public became aware of the aborted coup and the resignation from Republican leadership of a promising young conservative, Representative Bill Paxon of New York.

A group of conservatives said they spoke with Gingrich's top deputies July 10 about replacing Gingrich with a person who would take a harder line with the White House on budget and tax issues. Paxon denied he was party to the plot but said his discussions with the group cost him the speaker's trust.

House Republican Leader Dick Armey of Texas told reporters Friday he had stepped in to quell the rebellion as soon as he learned of its existence. Republican Whip Tom DeLay of Texas has had little to say about his role and issued a statement last week that he did not intend to resign his post.
As Gingrich tried to rally his team, Republicans will be testing his performance in negotiations with the White House and Democrats on tax and spending bills.

But there was danger that pressure to push these bills further to the party's right by insisting on indexing of capital gains tax rates for inflation and seeking a smaller child tax credit, might forfeit passage of these key bills.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said the events of the past week in the House have contributed to a gloomy outlook for passage of the bills by the August recess.

"It appears that all of the talk and concern about revolution in the House has caused some of our Republican colleagues to attempt to placate the far right of their caucus in the House, and that is not going to get us an agreement," Daschle said.
Party rebels said the failed move against Gingrich had come sooner than expected because of encouragement from at least one party leader, and several said that person was DeLay.

"And frankly, were it not for the fact that we felt that there were members of leadership, or at least a member of leadership, that was moving to replace the speaker, we would not have taken any action last week," Representative Matt Salmon of Arizona said on ABC television's "This Week."

Paxon was the only one of the Republican leaders appointed by Gingrich. The others were elected and thus report officially to the entire 228-member Republican conference and as one lawmaker said, there will be larger attendance than usual this week at the conference's regular Wednesday meeting.
